t.2.33.1: Having heard the words of the chief minister, Rāma, who knew what modesty requires, then addressed Daśaratha in speech, as one who is humble.
t.2.33.2: O king, what need have I of a retinue, I who have given up all enjoyments, who will live in the forest on forest fare, and who have renounced attachment on every side?
t.2.33.3: For one who, having given away the finest of elephants, still sets his mind on its girth-rope, what use is attachment to the rope when he is giving up the best of elephants?
t.2.33.4: So too, O best of the virtuous, O lord of the world, what use have I for an army? I relinquish everything; let them bring me only garments of bark.
t.2.33.5: Bring me both a spade and a basket, for I am going away to make my dwelling in the forest for fourteen years.
t.2.33.6: Then Kaikeyī, shameless before the throng of people, herself brought garments of bark and said to Rāghava, "Put these on."
t.2.33.7: When they had received the two bark garments from Kaikeyī, that tiger among men cast off his fine clothing and dressed himself in the garments of a sage.
t.2.33.9: Then Sītā, who was clad in silk, seeing the bark garment meant for her own wearing, was terrified, like a doe at the sight of a snare.
t.2.33.8: Lakṣmaṇa too, right there in front of his father, cast off his two fine garments and took two coverings from an ascetic.
t.2.33.11: Placing one bark garment at her throat and taking the other in her hand, Janaka's daughter stood there, unskilled in wearing it and filled with shame.
t.2.33.10: Receiving it, Sītā, distressed and as if ashamed, said this to her husband, who resembled the king of the gandharvas: "How indeed do the sages tie on the bark garment of a forest-dweller?"
t.2.33.12: Quickly approaching her, Rāma, the best of those who uphold dharma, himself tied that bark garment over Sītā's silken robe.
t.2.33.13: As she, who had a protector, put on the bark garment as though she had none, all the people cried out, "Shame on you, Daśaratha!"
t.2.33.14: Sighing hotly, the Aikṣvāka said this to his wife: "Kaikeyi, Sītā ought not to go clad in a garment of kuśa grass."
t.2.33.15: Surely this banishment of Rāma is enough for you, O wicked woman! What more is to be gained by these wretched sinful deeds you are committing besides?
t.2.33.16: To his father, who spoke thus as he sat with his head bowed down, Rāma, who had set out for the forest, spoke these words.
t.2.33.17: O righteous one, this is Kausalyā, my illustrious mother, aged and of a character free from meanness, and she does not ... you, O woman reviled by the gods.
t.2.33.18: O bestower of boons, you ought to honor her once more, bereft of me as she is, sunk in an ocean of grief, she who has never before known such misfortune.
t.2.33.19: You ought to treat this mother of mine, who bore in her womb a son like great Indra, in such a way that, while I dwell in the forest, she, wasted by grief, does not abandon her life and go to the abode of Yama.
